source.module_title: Keil and Delitzsch Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.1-2Chr.19.3">2Ch 19:1-3</reference> <hi type="italic">The prophet Jehu’s declaration as to Jehoshaphat’s alliance with Ahab, and Jehoshaphat’s further efforts to promote the fear of God and the administration of justice in Judah</hi>. - <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.1">2Ch 19:1</reference>-3. Jehu’s declaration. Jehoshaphat returned from the war in which Ahab had lost his life, בּשׁלום, i.e., safe, uninjured, to his house in Jerusalem; so that the promise of Micah in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="2Chr.18.16">2Ch 18:16</reference></hi> was fulfilled also as regards him. But on his return, the seer Jehu, the son of Hanani, who had been thrown into the stocks by Asa (2Ch 16:7.), met him with the reproving word, “Should one help the wicked, and lovest thou the haters of Jahve!” (the inf. with ל, as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.5.1">1Ch 5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.25">1Ch 9:25</reference>, etc.). Of these sins Jehoshaphat had been guilty. “And therefore is anger from Jahve upon thee” (על קצף as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.24">1Ch 27:24</reference>). Jehoshaphat had already had experience of this wrath, when in the battle of Ramoth the enemy pressed upon him (<reference osisRef="2Chr.18.31">2Ch 18:31</reference>), and was at a later time to have still further experience of it, partly during his own life, when the enemy invaded his land (2 Chron 20), and when he attempted to re-establish the sea trade with Ophir (2Ch 20:35.), partly after his death in his family (2 Chron 21 and <reference osisRef="2Chr.22.1-2Chr.22.12">2Ch 22:1-12</reference>). “But,” continues Jehu, to console him, “yet there are good things found in thee (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.12">2Ch 12:12</reference>), for thou hast destroyed the Asheroth...” אשׁרות = אשׁרים, 2Ch 17:6. On these last words, comp. <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.14">2Ch 12:14</reference> and 2Ch 17:4.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.4">2Ch 19:4</reference> <hi type="italic">Jehoshaphat’s further arrangements for the revival of the Jahve-worship, and the establishment of a proper administration of justice</hi>. - The first two clauses in <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.4">2Ch 19:4</reference> are logically connected thus: When Jehoshaphat (after his return from the war) sat (dwelt) in Jerusalem, he again went forth (ויּצא ויּשׁב are to be taken together) among the people, from Beersheba, the southern frontier (see <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.2">1Ch 21:2</reference>), to Mount Ephraim, the northern frontier of the kingdom of Judah, and brought them back to Jahve, the God of the fathers. The “<hi type="italic">again</hi>” (ישׁב) can refer only to the former provision for the instruction of the people, recorded in 2Ch 17:7.; all that was effected by the commission which Jehoshaphat had sent throughout the land being regarded as his work. The instruction of the people in the law was intended to lead them back to the Lord. Jehoshaphat now again took up his work of reformation, in order to complete the work he had begun, by ordering and improving the administration of justice.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.5-2Chr.19.7">2Ch 19:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen6045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6046" type="x-p"/> He set judges in the land, in all the fenced cities of Judah; they, as larger cities, being centres of communication for their respective neighbourhoods, and so best suited to be the seats of judges. ועיר לעיר, in reference to every city, as the law (<reference osisRef="Deut.16.18">Deu 16:18</reference>) prescribed. He laid it upon the consciences of these judges to administer justice conscientiously. “Not for men are ye to judge, but for Jahve;” i.e., not on the appointment and according to the will of men, but in the name and according to the will of the Lord (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.16.11">Pro 16:11</reference>). In the last clause of <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.6">2Ch 19:6</reference>, Jahve is to be supplied from the preceding context: “and Jahve is with you in judgment,” i.e., in giving your decisions (cf. the conclusion of <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.11">2Ch 19:11</reference>); whence this clause, of course, only serves to strengthen the foregoing, only contains the thoughts already expressed in the law, that judgment belongs to God (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.1.17">Deu 1:17</reference> with <reference osisRef="Exod.21.6">Exo 21:6</reference>; Exo 22:7.). Therefore the fear of the Lord should keep the judges from unrighteousness, so that they should neither allow themselves to be influenced by respect of persons, nor to be bribed by gifts, against which <reference osisRef="Deut.16.19">Deu 16:19</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.1.17">Deu 1:17</reference> also warns. ועשׂוּ שׁמרוּ is rightly paraphrased by the Vulgate, <hi type="italic">cum diligentia cuncta facite</hi>. The clause, “With God there is no respect of persons,” etc., recalls Deu 10:17.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.8-2Chr.19.11">2Ch 19:8-11</reference> <div eID="gen6046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6047" type="x-p"/> Besides this, Jehoshaphat established at Jerusalem a supreme tribunal for the decision of difficult cases, which the judges of the individual cities could not decide. 2Ch 19:8. “Moreover, in Jerusalem did Jehoshaphat set certain of the Levites, and of the priests, and of the chiefs of the fathers'-houses of Israel, for the judgment of the Lord, and for controversies (לריב).” From this clause Berth. correctly draws the conclusion, that as in Jerusalem, so also in the fenced cities (<reference osisRef="2Chr.19.5">2Ch 19:5</reference>), it was Levites, priests, and heads of the fathers'-houses who were made judges. This conclusion is not inconsistent with the fact that David appointed 6000 of the Levites to be shoterim and judges; for it does not follow from that that none but Levites were appointed judges, but only that the Levites were to perform an essential part in the administration of the law. The foundation of the judicial body in Israel was the appointment of judges chosen from the elders of the people (Exo 18:21.; Deu 1:15.) by Moses, at Jethro’s instigation, and under the divine sanction, David had no intention, by his appointment of some thousands of Levites to be officials (writers) and judges, to set aside the Mosaic arrangement; on the contrary, he thereby gave it the expansion which the advanced development of the kingdom required. For the simple relationships of the Mosaic time, the appointment of elders to be judges might have been sufficient; but when in the course of time, especially after the introduction of the kingship, the social and political relations became more complicated, it is probable that the need of appointing men with special skill in law, to co-operate with the judges chosen from among the elders, in order that justice might be administered in a right way, and in a manner corresponding to the law, made itself increasingly felt; that consequently David had felt himself called upon to appoint a greater number of Levites to this office, and that from that time forward the courts in the larger cities were composed of Levites and elders. The supreme court which Jehoshaphat set up in Jerusalem was established on a similar basis. For יהוה למשׁפּט we have in <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.11">2Ch 19:11</reference> דּבר־יהוה לכל, i.e., for all matters connected with religion and the worship and instead of קריב we have המּלך דּבר לכל, for every matter of the king, i.e., for all civil causes. The last clause, <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.8">2Ch 19:8</reference>, ירוּשׁלים ויּשׁבוּ, cannot signify that the men called to this supreme tribunal went to Jerusalem to dwell there thenceforth (Ramb., etc.), or that the suitors went thither; for שׁוּב does not denote to betake oneself to a place, but to return, which cannot be said of the persons above named, since it is not said that they had left Jerusalem. With Kimchi and others, we must refer the words to the previous statement in <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.4">2Ch 19:4</reference>, וגו בּעם ויּצא, and understand them as a supplementary statement, that Jehoshaphat and those who had gone forth with him among the people returned to Jerusalem, which would have come in more fittingly at the close of <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.7">2Ch 19:7</reference>, and is to be rendered: “when they had returned to Jerusalem.” The bringing in of this remark at so late a stage of the narrative, only after the establishment of the supreme tribunal has been mentioned, is explained by supposing that the historian was induced by the essential connection between the institution of the supreme court and the arrangement of the judicatories in the provincial cities, to leave out of consideration the order of time in describing the arrangements made by Jehoshaphat.
